agent: frontier-second: the next two most-called unnamed functions in the image
question: 0x65A7A0 (42 named callers) and 0x6647D0 (40), both high in the same population as sscanf and atoi and both reached from *::LoadKey. What are they, what are their signatures and calling conventions, and can they be named?

addresses.name: std::string::fromCString
addresses.signature: Hoi3CString* __cdecl std::string::fromCString(Hoi3CString* this@ESI, const char* text@EDX)
addresses.comment: MSVC's `std::basic_string<char>::basic_string(const char*)`, statically linked and given a register calling convention by LTCG: the string is in ESI and the C string in EDX, nothing is on the stack, and `this` comes back in EAX. The body is the textbook two steps. First `_Tidy()` on an *uninitialised* object - `[esi+0x14] = 0xF` (_Myres), `[esi+0x10] = 0` (_Mysize), `[esi] = 0` (_Buf[0]), the same 0x18-byte layout `std::string::assign` at 0xA160 already reads. Then `assign(_Ptr, _Traits::length(_Ptr))`: a four-instruction inline strlen (`lea edi,[eax+1]` / `mov cl,[eax]; inc eax; test cl,cl; jne` / `sub eax,edi`) whose result is pushed with the pointer before `mov ecx,esi; call 0xA160`. **6732 direct call sites**, far more than any other unnamed function left, and it is how every loader, log line and error message turns a literal into a string - the caller is invariably `mov edx,<literal>; lea esi,<fresh local>; call`, followed by the EH state byte being stepped for the new object. There is no null check on EDX, which is what separates the constructor from an assignment.
addresses.evidence: Machine checks, three of them. (1) The convention: 60 call sites sampled at random, decoded from their own function start rather than backwards, and all 36 that decode cleanly set both ESI and EDX in the twelve instructions before the call, none pushes an argument, none cleans the stack afterwards, and the body ends in a bare `ret` - so __cdecl with two register arguments and zero stack bytes, which checkSignatures confirms against the ret. (2) The callee: 0x40A160 is already `std::string::assign(this, char* text, uint length)` in project.json, and the push order here (len, then ptr, ecx=this) is exactly that signature. (3) The _Tidy constants 0xF/0/0 at +0x14/+0x10/+0 are the MSVC small-buffer string with a 16-byte buffer, and the wide-character twin immediately after at 0x65A7D0 builds the same object with `_Myres = 7` and a `word ptr` scan loop, which is what the same source compiles to for wchar_t. **What would show it wrong:** a call site that passes an already-live string in ESI (this would then be `assign`, not a constructor, and the missing free would be a leak), or ESI holding something that is not the 0x18-byte string layout - neither appeared in the sample. vtable.py --holding reports it in no class's virtual table, so it is a free function, not a folded virtual.

addresses.name: LogRecord::FlushAndDestruct
addresses.comment: The body of `~LogRecord` - the destructor of the ostringstream-derived temporary every log line in the game is built into, inlined at 679 call sites. **Its argument is not the record: it is `record + 0x78`**, the `std::basic_ios` virtual base, and every field is reached at a negative displacement from it, so a reader has to subtract 0x78 to get back to the object. It (1) writes the basic_ios vftable 0x15FCE94 through the vbtable at `record+0`, (2) calls 0x65BD10 to pull `str()` out of the stringbuf at `record+4`, (3) copies that into a second local string with `std::string::assign`, (4) makes the sink call `(*(*[record+0x50]))[1](channel=[record+0x74], file=record+0x54, line=[record+0x70], message=&text)` - slot 1 of the sink at `record+0x50`, which FINDINGS-script.md already records as `LogSink::Write(channel, file, line, message)` with exactly that field layout, (5) frees both temporaries and (6) tears the stream back down, vftable 0x15FC550 for the ios base, 0x15F2B34 on the stringbuf before 0x6D1360 and 0x10CD90 destroy it, and 0x15A7B94 last. It does **not** run the final `ios_base` destructor; the caller does, which is why `LogRecord::Flush` at 0x24B0 is only `lea esi,[eax+0x78]; push esi; call this; mov [esi],0x15A7B8C; call 0x794BAE` and why all 679 inline sites repeat that same two-step tail. This is the reason the two targets share so many *::LoadKey callers without sharing all of them: 0x65A7A0 builds the message, this one emits it.
addresses.evidence: (1) Convention: the body ends `ret 4`, and of 60 sampled call sites the 56 that decode cleanly all push exactly one pointer before the call and none does `add esp,4` after it - __stdcall with one stack argument, which checkSignatures confirms. (2) Identity: the four displacements it reads off the argument, -0x28/-0x24/-8/-4 against an argument of record+0x78, are record+0x50, +0x54, +0x70, +0x74, which is the sink / source file / line / channel layout FINDINGS-script.md established for LogRecord from the other end (LogRecord::LogRecord at 0x2464E0), and the indirect call takes slot 1 with those four in LogSink::Write's order. (3) The already-named `LogRecord::Flush` (0x24B0) calls this function and nothing else, passing record+0x78, which ties the argument to the record with no inference. (4) The vbptr/vbtable idiom `mov eax,[obj]; mov edx,[eax+4]; mov [edx+obj],<vftable>` at both ends is MSVC's virtual-base vftable store, and the offset it computes is 0x78, matching where the argument points. **What would show it wrong:** a call site whose argument minus 0x78 is not a LogRecord - e.g. some other ostringstream-derived class reusing this body - which would show up as a sink pointer at +0x50 whose slot 1 is not LogSink::Write; or LogSink::Write's argument order being other than (channel, file, line, message), which would make the four reads land on different fields. Both are checkable and neither failed. vtable.py --holding reports it in no class's virtual table.

slots_noted: Neither function appears in any class's virtual table (vtable.py --holding, both), so there is no slot to record. Frontier notes: 0x65BD10 is a two-instruction thunk (`mov esi,eax; add ecx,4; call 0x520940; mov eax,esi`) that looks like ostringstream::str() forwarding to the stringbuf's str() at 0x520940 - 0x520940 is one step past the direct callees and is the thing actually worth naming. 0x6D1360 is entered with the stringbuf in ESI and frees its buffer, i.e. basic_stringbuf::_Tidy; 0x10CD90 is __thiscall on the same object, writes vftable 0x15A7BE4 and frees the rest, i.e. its destructor. Not named here: they are STL bodies reached only through this one function, and naming them properly wants the ostringstream layout done as a whole. Also unnamed but not called by either target: 0x794BAE, the ios_base destructor the caller runs after FlushAndDestruct.
